scores.evidence: Lag p99 ≤ 5 s at the baseline peak (ASSUMPTION: catch-up must fit inside the write pause).
scores.rationale: Technical claims (log-based replication, fencing, synchronous AZ copies for RPO 0, UTC/DST appointment-time risk, DNS TTL) are accurate and state real limits precisely, with fallbacks where tooling might not behave as assumed.

scores.evidence: "No downtime" allows a short write pause. It means reads never stop and writes may pause for a few seconds
scores.rationale: Resolves the key ambiguity of 'no downtime' explicitly and requires clinical sign-off on it; the staged lift-and-shift is clearly buildable, and all deferrals are explicit with pull-forward triggers.

scores.evidence: Exactly one writable database at all times: on-premises until the switch, cloud after. Replication runs one way. The old side is fenced read-only.
scores.rationale: The single-writer decision, batch-job single-node constraint, PHI boundary and phase gates are honored consistently across phases, validation checks, and runbook steps with no contradictions.

scores.evidence: ≥ 2 consecutive full rehearsals with synthetic bookings during the switch. Fencing test. Reverse switch. Then a go/no-go meeting.
scores.rationale: Each risk has a named check (V0-V7) with measurable thresholds, assumptions labeled and requiring confirmation, riskiest items validated before commitment, and post-cutover SLO monitoring continues validation in production.

scores.evidence: Assumptions this plan rests on. Each one says what changes if it is false.
scores.rationale: Assumptions are explicit, labeled (REQUIREMENT/ASSUMPTION/BASELINE/UNKNOWN), ranked missing inputs are listed, and every budget and threshold states who confirms it and what changes if it is wrong.

scores.evidence: the post-switch reconciliation shows 0 lost or duplicated appointments; HL7 counts match
scores.rationale: Covers the hardest domain failures—dual-write double-booking, replication loss, DST/timezone corruption, zone and circuit failure, missed consumers, HL7 gaps/duplicates—each with concrete detection, containment and rehearsed recovery.

scores.evidence: a deploy and a rollback both succeed through the pipeline; stopping the app service fires the alert within 5 min
scores.rationale: Deployment, rollback, migration, meaningful health signals, named decision owners, CAB process and a 90-day dual-operations cap make the burden explicit and plausible for a hospital IT team.

scores.evidence: Reserved capacity or savings plans. Pulled forward after 30 days of cost data after the switch, checked against the Finance budget.
scores.rationale: Cost is treated honestly as an UNKNOWN with concrete controls (right-sizing, cost dashboard, data-gated reserved capacity, Finance budget gate), but cost drivers and orders of magnitude are never enumerated or estimated.

scores.evidence: Stop reverse replication. This is the point of no return.
scores.rationale: Every key decision carries an R2/R3 reversibility rating with a revisit trigger, irreversible steps (switch, decommission) are gated and rehearsed, and reversible choices (Terraform, TTLs) are made quickly as minor defaults.

scores.evidence: Lift the app tier as-is onto VMs. Same database engine and major version... No re-architecture.
scores.rationale: The simplest design that meets the no-downtime need; re-architecture, autoscaling, active-active and new features are explicitly deferred with pull-forward conditions, and nothing essential is omitted.

Phases have ordered tasks, checkable exit criteria, dependency reasoning, and explicit contingency paths for every failed validation, so a team could start Phase 0 immediately without redoing the thinking.

checklist.evidence: PHI only in services the BAA covers, in one in-country region. Private endpoints only, customer-managed keys. Logs and telemetry with PHI stay inside the boundary.
HL7 appointment and patient-registration feeds, portal, SMS/IVR reminders, billing, warehouse ETL, direct database readers (reporting tools), file drops, printers and kiosks
Seed it from a backup. Start one-way replication... Run a daily reconciliation: row counts plus per-table hashes
Exactly one writable database at all times: on-premises until the switch, cloud after... The old side is fenced read-only.
At the switch, start reverse replication (cloud → on-premises) and keep on-premises warm and read-only until V7.
Two private circuits on diverse paths plus an IPsec VPN backup... The app tolerates the extra network round-trip time | V4
RPO 0 for committed bookings; writes resume ≤ 60 s after a zone failure... downtime procedures on standby
they stay on the existing Active Directory / SSO... MFA plus just-in-time admin — but audited break-glass access is never defined
Load at 2× peak for 2 h on a production-sized copy. Kill a zone. Pull the primary circuit.
Pick a low-volume window from the baseline (for example Sunday 02:00)... Start 14 days of close support.
Vendor support statement and license portability... Decommission, with media sanitized to NIST 800-88.

traps.evidence: Move user groups to the cloud app tier in this order: IT → one low-volume clinic → one department → call center → everyone
No database with two writers. During a network split, only the primary side takes writes.
PHI in the cloud is covered by contract and controls before any of it arrives
The interface engine queues messages instead of sending them... Turn on the interface engine's cloud endpoints and drain its queues.
the app stays one unit, not split into services. Changing that is a re-architecture project.

note: An exemplary, near-reference migration plan: single-writer discipline, rehearsed reversible cutover, labeled assumptions and risk-first validation; only notable gaps are undefined break-glass access and absent cost magnitudes.
